concepts.name: GDP: Definition, Scope and Territorial Boundary
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'domestic territory' vs 'geographic territory' (embassies, ships, military bases)
Inclusion of output by foreign residents within borders vs exclusion of output by nationals abroad
Why GDP is a 'flow' concept measured over a period, not a stock
UPSC trap: whether embassy of India in USA is part of India's domestic territory

concepts.name: GNP: Nationality Principle and Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)
key_dimensions: Formula: GNP = GDP + NFIA (can be positive or negative)
Components of NFIA: wages of residents working abroad, profits of MNCs repatriated, interest on foreign loans
Why GNP > GDP for capital-exporting countries (USA) and GNP < GDP for capital-importing countries (India historically)
UPSC trap: distinguishing 'factor income' from 'transfer payments' (remittances are NOT factor income in strict sense)

concepts.name: NNP: Role of Depreciation (Capital Consumption Allowance)
key_dimensions: Formula: NNP = GNP − Depreciation; NNP reflects true net addition to national wealth
Why NNP is considered a better welfare measure than GNP/GDP
Depreciation vs amortization vs obsolescence: what is included in national income accounting
UPSC trap: NNP at Market Price vs NNP at Factor Cost (= National Income) — the indirect tax/subsidy adjustment

concepts.name: National Income (NI) at Factor Cost vs Market Price
key_dimensions: Formula: NI (FC) = NNP (MP) − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies
Why factor cost reflects actual returns to factors of production, stripping out government distortions
Recent India shift: CSO moved from GDP at Factor Cost to GVA at Basic Prices as primary measure (2015 revision)
UPSC trap: 'Basic Price' is NOT the same as 'Factor Cost' — basic price includes production taxes/subsidies but excludes product taxes

concepts.name: GVA at Basic Prices: India's Current Methodology
key_dimensions: GVA (Basic Price) = GVA (FC) + Production taxes − Production subsidies
GDP (MP) = Sum of GVA (Basic Prices) + Product taxes − Product subsidies
Why India shifted from GDP at Factor Cost to GVA at Basic Prices in 2015 base year revision
UPSC trap: GVA ≠ GDP; GDP = GVA + Net Product Taxes — students often conflate the two

concepts.name: Expenditure Method of GDP Calculation
key_dimensions: Formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); each component defined precisely
What counts as 'Investment' (I): fixed capital formation + change in inventories, NOT financial investment
Government expenditure (G): only current expenditure on goods/services, NOT transfer payments
UPSC trap: net exports can be negative (import-heavy economies); transfer payments like pensions are NOT included

concepts.name: Income Method of GDP Calculation
key_dimensions: Components: compensation of employees + gross operating surplus + gross mixed income + net taxes on production
Distinction between 'compensation of employees' (wages + social contributions) vs self-employment income
Why transfer payments (unemployment benefits, pensions) are excluded from income method
UPSC trap: imputed rent of owner-occupied houses IS included; illegal activities are excluded

concepts.name: Output/Value Added Method and Avoiding Double Counting
key_dimensions: Value Added = Value of Output − Value of Intermediate Consumption at each stage
Why final goods approach and value-added approach give identical results
Three sectors: primary, secondary, tertiary — boundary issues (e.g., is software a good or service?)
UPSC trap: sale of second-hand goods is NOT included (no new production); only broker's commission is counted

concepts.name: Transfer Payments: Exclusion Logic and Boundary Cases
key_dimensions: Definition: one-way payment with no corresponding production (pensions, scholarships, remittances, doles)
Why transfer payments are excluded from GDP but included in personal income calculations
Boundary case: are government subsidies transfer payments? (production subsidies vs consumption subsidies)
UPSC trap: foreign remittances by Indian diaspora — excluded from GDP/GNP factor income but affect personal disposable income

concepts.name: Personal Income (PI) and Personal Disposable Income (PDI)
key_dimensions: Formula: PI = NI − Corporate taxes − Retained earnings − Social security contributions + Transfer payments
PDI = PI − Personal direct taxes
Why PI can exceed NI (due to transfer payments) — UPSC frequently tests this counterintuitive point
Distinction: PDI is the actual spending/saving power, most relevant for consumption function in Keynesian economics

concepts.name: GDP vs GNP: Which is a Better Measure for India?
key_dimensions: For capital-importing developing nations, GDP > GNP historically (profits repatriated by MNCs exceed remittances in some periods)
Post-2000s India: large remittance inflows (world's largest recipient) mean NFIA has turned more complex
Policy relevance: GDP for domestic production tracking; GNP for national welfare and standard of living
UPSC trap: Ireland's GDP >> GNP due to massive MNC profit repatriation — classic example of divergence

concepts.name: Real vs Nominal GDP: GDP Deflator
key_dimensions: Nominal GDP: at current prices; Real GDP: at constant (base year) prices — removes inflation effect
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100; differs from CPI/WPI in coverage
GDP Deflator covers ALL goods/services in economy; CPI covers consumer basket only
UPSC trap: GDP Deflator can differ significantly from CPI — e.g., if capital goods prices rise but consumer prices stable

concepts.name: Base Year Revision in National Income Accounting (India: 2011-12)
key_dimensions: India's current base year is 2011-12 (revised from 2004-05); captures structural changes in economy
Key changes: introduction of MCA-21 database for corporate sector, better coverage of unorganized sector
Shift from GDP at Factor Cost → GVA at Basic Prices as headline measure
UPSC trap: base year revision often leads to upward revision of GDP growth rates — 2015 controversy when India's growth appeared to exceed China's

concepts.name: Green GDP / Environmentally Adjusted Net National Product
key_dimensions: Green GDP = GDP − Cost of environmental degradation − Depletion of natural resources
Rationale: traditional GDP rewards pollution cleanup as positive (Broken Window Fallacy applied to environment)
India's attempts: ENRAP (Environment and Natural Resource Accounting Project); challenges in monetizing ecosystem services
UPSC trap: Green GDP is lower than conventional GDP; a country with high GDP growth but resource depletion may have low/negative Green GDP

concepts.name: GDP and Welfare: Limitations as a Measure of Well-being
key_dimensions: GDP ignores: income distribution (Gini coefficient), unpaid household work, leisure, environmental quality
Simon Kuznets (GDP's architect) himself warned it should not be used as a welfare measure
Alternatives: HDI, GNH (Gross National Happiness — Bhutan), Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)
UPSC trap: higher GDP per capita does NOT necessarily mean higher welfare — Kerala paradox (lower GDP, higher HDI than many richer states)

concepts.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) vs Gross Capital Formation (GCF)
key_dimensions: GFCF = investment in fixed assets (machinery, buildings, infrastructure) — excludes inventory changes
GCF = GFCF + Change in inventories + Net acquisition of valuables
GFCF as % of GDP is a key indicator of productive capacity building; India's GFCF declining trend post-2012 is a concern
UPSC trap: financial investments (buying stocks/bonds) are NOT part of GFCF — only physical/real capital creation counts

concepts.name: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) vs Market Exchange Rate for GDP Comparison
key_dimensions: PPP adjusts for price level differences across countries; market rate reflects currency market forces
India's GDP rank: ~5th by market exchange rate but ~3rd by PPP (IMF data) — reflects lower price levels in India
Big Mac Index as a simplified PPP illustration; ICP (International Comparison Program) for official PPP
UPSC trap: PPP comparison is better for welfare/standard of living comparison; market rate better for international trade/debt analysis

concepts.name: Informal/Unorganized Sector Estimation Challenges in GDP
key_dimensions: India's informal sector ~45-50% of GDP but poorly measured; relies on extrapolation from periodic surveys (NSS)
Demonetization 2016: debates on whether GDP captured informal sector contraction accurately
NSSO surveys (now NSO) vs ASI (Annual Survey of Industries) — different coverage and frequency
UPSC trap: MCA-21 data used for organized corporate sector may overestimate overall GDP if informal sector shrinks; leading to GDP paradox during slowdowns

concepts.name: Savings, Investment Identity and GDP: Macroeconomic Balance
key_dimensions: Closed economy: S = I; Open economy: S − I = X − M (current account balance)
National Savings = Private Savings + Government Savings (fiscal surplus/deficit affects national savings)
India's high household savings rate historically financed investment; declining household savings post-2020 is a concern
UPSC trap: fiscal deficit 'crowds out' private investment through higher interest rates — but in developing economies with surplus savings, this may not hold

concepts.name: Chain-Linking Method vs Fixed Base Year in GDP Calculation
key_dimensions: Fixed base year: simple but becomes outdated as economic structure changes; requires periodic revision
Chain-linking: updates weights every year using Fisher's ideal index — used by USA, UK; more accurate but complex
India still uses fixed base year method — limitation acknowledged by CSO/NSO
UPSC trap: with fixed base year, sectors that grew rapidly (IT services post-1991) were underweighted in old base year, leading to underestimation of growth
